## Findability comes from description

A Zenodo record with a bare title and no keywords is a catalog record with no subject headings: retrievable if you already know it exists, invisible if you don't.

The tools are GitHub topics, Zenodo fields, and a README. The question is the same: *what would a seeker search for, and does this record contain it?*

You already have a license, a CITATION.cff, and a DOI. **This episode ties them together.**

::: {.notes}

and five minutes of description decides whether anyone ever finds it. Libraries
already know how to do this: it's cataloging.
:::

## What counts as useful metadata?

Good metadata answers predictable questions with minimal effort from the reader:

- **What is this software?** A short description or abstract
- **Who made it?** Authors and ORCIDs
- **How do I cite it?** CITATION.cff and a DOI
- **What field is it for?** Keywords
- **What else does it relate to?** A related article, dataset, or funder

::: {.notes}
**~2 min · SHOW:** slides only.

**SAY:** Every one of these answers a question someone will ask. Then the authority
control point: title, authors, and description should read the same in the README,
CITATION.cff, and Zenodo. When they drift, indexes treat one piece of software as
several, and its citations scatter.
:::

## Add GitHub Topics

On your repo's front page, click the **gear icon next to About**, then fill in **Topics**:

- **Discipline:** `geospatial`, `text-mining`, `materials-science`
- **Method:** `simulation`, `visualization`, `machine-learning`
- **Language:** `python`, `r`

![](images/repository-topics.png){fig-align="center" height="380"}

::: {.notes}
**~3 min · LIVE DEMO, then learners do it**

**DO** (tab 1, prepared repo):

1. On the repo front page, find **About** in the right sidebar and click the **gear icon**
2. **Description:** Analysis tools for biodiversity research data
3. **Topics:** type biodiversity, research-software, python (press space after each)
4. Click **Save changes**

**SHOW:** the topics appear as chips under About. Click one to show GitHub's topic
search page, then come back.

**SAY:** Reuse these same words later in CITATION.cff and Zenodo. Consistency is the point.
Give learners 1 minute to add topics to their own fork.
:::

## The 30-second rule

**Your README is your software's front door.**

If people can't tell what it does, how to install it, and how to use it in **30 seconds**, they leave.

A repo without a real README is a collection without a finding aid: only its author can use it.

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · DO:** switch to the upstream repo's main branch README (bare).
**SHOW:** hold it for ten seconds. Ask: could you install and run this from what's here?
Then back to the slides.

**SAY:** A repo without a real README is a collection without a finding aid.
:::

## README: 7 essential sections

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
1. **About:** what it does, in 2-3 sentences
2. **Features:** key capabilities
3. **Getting Started:** prerequisites and install
4. **Usage:** a minimal working example
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
5. **Citation:** link to CITATION.cff or the DOI
6. **License:** state the terms
7. **Contact:** how to get help
:::

::::

::: {.small}
[UC OSPO README Guide](https://ucospo.net/oss-resources/template-guides/readme-guide/) *(UC-specific)*
:::

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · SHOW:** slides only. Walk the 7 quickly; don't explain each one in depth,
the next challenge does that.

**SAY:** The UC OSPO README guide has a template (link in the Etherpad).
:::

## Before → after

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
**❌ Before** (`main`, starting state)

```markdown
# Biodiversity Analysis Toolkit

Analysis tools for biodiversity
research data.
```

One line of description. No install steps, no usage, no citation, no license, no one to contact.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
**✅ After** (`05-add-metadata`, abridged)

```markdown
# Biodiversity Analysis Toolkit
[DOI badge] [License badge]
Analysis tools for biodiversity...   <!-- 1 About -->

## Features                          <!-- 2 -->
- Citable, open source, documented

## Getting Started                   <!-- 3 -->
Prerequisites: Python 3.9+
### Installation & Usage             <!-- 4 -->
pip install -r requirements.txt
python src/analysis.py

## Citation                          <!-- 5 -->
Cite via CITATION.cff or the DOI badge.
## License                           <!-- 6 -->
BSD 3-Clause. See LICENSE.
## Contact                           <!-- 7 -->
Open an issue in this repository.
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
**~2 min · DO:** tab 2 (upstream, 05-add-metadata branch). Scroll the real README.

**SHOW:** point at each section and call out its number from the slide (1 to 7).
Usage is folded into Getting Started, which is common and fine. Point out the
extra sections too: Contributing, Code of Conduct, Authors.

**SAY:** Yours should look roughly like this now. This is the R in FAIR, in practice.
:::

## Beyond the README: community health files {background-color="#f0f4fa"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}
**CONTRIBUTING.md**\
How to contribute. Add one *if* you want contributions, or say plainly that you don't.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md**\
Behavioral standards. [Contributor Covenant][cc] is the standard choice.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**CHANGELOG.md**\
Version history: what's new, what broke, what changed.
:::

::::

[cc]: https://www.contributor-covenant.org/

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · DO:** tab 2, in the file list click **CONTRIBUTING.md**, then
**CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md**. A few seconds each.

**SAY:** CONTRIBUTING.md isn't always needed. Plenty of solid research software has
no contributor pipeline, and an invitation you can't follow up on creates more work
than it saves. "I'm not looking for contributors right now, please just open an
issue" is a complete, honest CONTRIBUTING.md.
:::

## GitHub recognizes certain filenames

| File | What GitHub does |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | Renders as the repository's landing page |
| `LICENSE` | Shows the license in the repo sidebar |
| `CITATION.cff` | Adds "Cite this repository" with APA/BibTeX |
| `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` | Counts toward the community profile |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md` | Links guidelines when someone opens an issue/PR |
| `SECURITY.md` | Becomes the security policy |

::: {.small}
These only appear once the file is on the default branch. GitHub changes the details, so teach the pattern: the filename is the signal.
:::

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · DO:** tab 1 (prepared repo). Point at the right sidebar.

**SHOW:** the **BSD-3-Clause** license badge and the **Cite this repository** link
(learners' forks have these from Karla's and Laura's episodes). Click Cite this repository to show
the APA and BibTeX it generates.

**SAY:** GitHub did this because of the filenames. That's the pattern to remember.
:::

## Where should software live? {background-color="#f0f4fa"}

**Zenodo is the recommended deposit location** for software:

- Archives each GitHub release automatically
- Mints a DOI for every version
- Registers records with DataCite, which discovery services harvest
- Free, run by CERN, recognized by journals and funders

Dataverse and Dryad are good for **datasets**, but don't auto-integrate with GitHub releases the same way.

::: {.small}
UC-specific: all UC campuses have Dryad. If you deposit data there, Dryad prompts a linked Zenodo code deposit automatically.
:::

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · SHOW:** slides only.

**SAY:** Zenodo for software because it archives each GitHub release. At UC, if
you deposit data in Dryad, Dryad prompts you to put the code in Zenodo too.
:::

## Zenodo metadata is what discovery systems see

Zenodo registers each record with **DataCite**. Search tools and discovery services pick it up from there, so the Zenodo record is what they show.

Add or refine: authors + ORCIDs, keywords, related works, funding, a readable description.

::: {.small}
**Caution:** if a repo has a `.zenodo.json`, Zenodo uses *that* file, not `CITATION.cff`. Keep them in sync or you'll publish two different citation records for the same software.
:::

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · DO:** tab 3 (your Zenodo Sandbox record).

**SHOW:** the record page: title, creators, description, keywords. Point out how
thin it is.

**SAY:** This record is what DataCite and discovery services see, not your README.
And the caution: if a repo has a .zenodo.json, Zenodo uses that instead of
CITATION.cff, so keep them in sync.
:::

## Supporting others: priority order when metadata is thin {background-color="#f0f4fa"}

1. A readable **description**, the biggest loss when it's missing
2. **Author ORCIDs**: without them, every J. Chen on Zenodo looks the same
3. **Keywords**, reused consistently across GitHub, CITATION.cff, Zenodo
4. **Related works**: link the software to its paper, dataset, and grant

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · SHOW:** slides only.

**SAY:** Thin metadata means the software never surfaces in the catalog. The
question here is whether anyone can find it at all. Librarians in the room will
often spot the gaps faster than the researchers do.
:::

## Challenge: improve your Zenodo record

::: {.project-badge}
⏱ 5 min
:::

Open your record on **Zenodo Sandbox** (sandbox.zenodo.org) from the release episode. Select **Edit**, and add:

- keywords
- author ORCIDs, if they're missing
- a real description
- *optional:* a related paper or funder, if you have one

::: {.fragment}
Save and publish the updated record when done.
:::

::: {.notes}
**~6 min · DEMO for 1 minute, then 5 minutes for learners.** Start a 5-minute timer.

**DO** (tab 3, your Sandbox record):

1. Click **Edit** (on the right side of the record page)
2. **Keywords:** add biodiversity, research-software, python (same words as your topics)
3. **Creators:** point at your ORCID. It's already there because CITATION.cff
   carried it into Zenodo, which is why Laura's episode matters. Learners whose
   CITATION.cff had no ORCID add theirs here
4. **Description:** paste your README's About paragraph
5. **Save draft**, then **Publish**

**SHOW:** the updated record.

**SAY:** Editing metadata doesn't mint a new DOI. The same DOI now has a better record.

**HELPERS:** watch for anyone on zenodo.org instead of sandbox.zenodo.org. Anyone
whose release didn't reach Zenodo in Reid's episode has no record: they watch your
screen, and helpers note who's stuck.
:::

## Challenge: which change makes it discoverable?

::: {.project-badge}
⏱ 3 min
:::

A tool has been public on GitHub for a year: one-line README, no topics, a Zenodo record with only a title. **Which single change matters most?**

A. Add collaborators\
B. Descriptive topics, matching keywords, and a description\
C. More frequent commits\
D. A shorter name

::: {.fragment}
**B.** People find software through its *description*. Commit activity doesn't help. It's the same reason a catalog record with no subject headings is nearly invisible.
:::

::: {.notes}
**~2 min · DO:** ask the room to answer A, B, C, or D in the Zoom chat. Give
them 30 seconds, then click to reveal.

**SAY:** B. People find software through its description.
:::

## Key points

- Description is what makes software findable, on GitHub, Zenodo, and beyond
- Keep it consistent across CITATION.cff, README, topics, and Zenodo: that's authority control

::: {.notes}
**~1 min · SAY** the two points. Remind the room the reference branches are there
if anyone fell behind; the finished README is on 05-add-metadata.
:::
